items.title: Borneo burning: Life on the frontline of South East Asia's toxic haze
items.summary: A "Super El Niño" has fuelled months-long fires in Indonesia, making hundreds of thousands of people sick.
items.content:
When the sun hits the smog enveloping Indonesian Borneo, it turns everything the colour of rust. Cars, houses and streets appear and disappear out of a dim russet fog. There are few better words than "apocalyptic" to describe the way this looks.

But it's at night, in the quiet darkness, that mother-of-three Dianyra Eka Nastiti grows most fearful.

"Sometimes at night my baby's chest makes a rattling sound," she says. "She was hospitalised for bronchopneumonia when she was just a month and a half old, and every single night I worry: Will my child cough tomorrow?

Nastiti lives in Palangkaraya, at the frontline of a months-long environmental catastrophe that has blanketed large parts of Southeast Asia in a toxic haze.

Wildfires have torched some 1.9 million hectares across Indonesia since the start of the year, according to open-access satellite platform Nusantara Atlas – an area roughly the size of the US state of New Jersey, or the entire landmass of Fiji. One million hectares are thought to have burned in September alone.

But the toxic fallout is larger still. Swathes of smouldering forest, swamp and peatlands have turned the air thick with microparticles and carbon monoxide, creating a noxious cloud that has swaddled Indonesia and drifted as far as Singapore, Malaysia and the Philippines.

As of mid-October, Indonesia's Health Ministry had recorded more than 277,000 cases of people suffering from chronic coughs and acute respiratory infections. More than 62,000 of those were infants and toddlers under the age of five.

"The forest fires have had a huge impact, especially on everyone's health," says 22-year-old Natari Victoria, who was admitted to a health centre in Palangkarya after suffering from a cough for more than a week.

"I have young cousins, including babies, who are coughing too. It's really taking a toll on them."

Haze and smoke from peat fires contain a complex mixture of pollutants that pose serious health risks to the human body.

Among these are tiny microparticles which can penetrate deep into the lungs and, in some cases, enter the bloodstream, causing inflammation, chronic lung diseases and increased risk of premature death.

Another concern is the toxic greenhouse gases that are being unleashed into the air.

"Here in Central Kalimantan, especially in Palangkaraya, the sky has turned yellow and hazy," says Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office. "So what are the residents actually breathing in? It's not fresh oxygen; it's carbon dioxide and pollutants. And what happens as a result? The body – specifically the brain – doesn't get enough oxygen."

Children, older adults and pregnant women are particularly vulnerable to the dangers of haze, especially during prolonged periods of exposure, when the health impacts can accumulate.

In places like Palangkarya, the official advice is to stay indoors and avoid going out. But Nastiti says this is unrealistic.

"I still need to buy vegetables, stock up on food, purchase school supplies, and take care of other necessities," she explains. "It's simply not possible, and I feel like the people who say things like that have no idea what is actually happening here."

Nastiti's utmost priority, however, is the health and wellbeing of her children. And when the haze grows heavy, she is quick to force them inside.

"With conditions being so unsafe, I have no choice," she says. "Our young children should be at the park, playing with their friends and going to school. Instead, they are locked inside the house."

Lola Macitri, a 37-year-old who lives in the rural village of Ramang, 50km (31 miles) north of Palangkaraya, has been similarly housebound. As the smog has deepened over the past few weeks – from dusty grey to amber yellow and, more recently, burnt orange – she and her family have come to spend most of their time indoors.

Her children, like many others in Indonesia's more haze-affected areas, have been doing their school classes online, she says, while she and other adults struggle to manage half-a-day's work out in the poisonous air.

Countless farmers, daily-wage earners and small vendors have similarly been forced to either sacrifice their livelihoods or endure the risk of stepping outside. Beyond that, many are left with no choice but to wait out the storm.

"If you ask whether we are afraid of the health risks, of course we are. But where else can we go?" says Macitri. "We just have to endure and stay strong through this situation, because there is simply no other option."

The government is under mounting pressure from the public to do more to stop the fires, with many criticising what they see as a woefully inadequate response by the authorities.

Authorities insist they have pursued a range of measures to try to extinguish the flames and, in turn, the smoke – from aerial waterbombing to experimental weather modification. Last week, the Indonesian government said it had deployed more than 60,000 personnel to carry out a "land operation", claiming they'd achieved an 80% success rate in extinguishing new fires.

"At this point, I think we need to use every safe and effective option available to suppress the fires," says Dr Nisa Novita, a forestry expert and peatland researcher at Indonesian conservation NGO Yayasan Konservasi Alam Nusantara (YKAN).

"It's a bit like trying to save a sinking ship: we need to act urgently, use whatever tools can help, and prevent further damage while we still can."

But those resources are fast depleting for responders on the ground.

For more than 100 days, Juni has been fighting wildfires that show only false signs of abating. On the surface, the flames are out – but underground, smouldering blazes continue to burn through a deep understory of carbon, vegetation and peat.

"It is truly exhausting," he says, describing how the relentless smoke has produced in him a shortness of breath, a persistent cough and an unshakeable pain in his eyes. When asked what he needs, he says "air".

"The haze makes it hard to breathe," he explains. "We are just hoping for heavy rain."

Thousands of others across Indonesia and Southeast Asia have spent the past several months hoping for the same.

Seasonal wildfires are not new to Indonesia but this year, a so-called Super El Nino has amplified drought conditions and delayed the kind of rainfall that is critical to extinguishing peat fires. It has also made things exponentially harder for those at the coalface, like Juni, who have spent months battling a seemingly irrepressible fire front.

Dr Novita explains that conditions on the ground have become much harsher even in recent weeks, as the prolonged drought makes water increasingly scarce.

Fauzi Rahman, another firefighter in Palangkaraya, highlighted this as one of the main difficulties confronting him and his peers.

"Peatland fires are hard to put out because they require a lot of water and a long time," he says. "On regular land we can clear 20 hectares in a single day, especially with a large team... On peatland, it can take months.

"We really have to inject water deep down, all the way to the bottom, which requires a huge amount of water. And right now, water is hard to find."

What's more concerning for Dr Novita, however, is that her team has reported fires spreading into areas where there has been no history of fire before.

"So we're not only dealing with fires in the usual hotspots but also seeing them emerge in new areas," she says.

In Palangkaraya, people are growing desperate for an end to this apocalypse. But it will likely take a force of nature for that to happen any time soon.

Riduan, head of the Palangkaraya Health Office, tells the BBC that "hopefully, with all the extraordinary efforts from the community, the military, and the police working together, the fires can be put out".

"However, as of right now, the fires are still burning," he adds. "So what can we hope for? Our greatest hope is that Almighty God will bring us rain soon."

The volunteers risking their lives to defuse Indonesia's wildfire 'carbon bombs'

items.title: The Other Epidemic: Trying to get off benzodiazepines
items.summary: https://web.archive.org/web/20261020230542/https://www.thebe... https://archive.ph/Tb1SZ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50173891 Points: 217 # Comments: 173
items.content:
Depersonalization, Brain Zaps, The Ashton Manual, GABA Receptors, BenzoBuddies, Purdue Pharma, Hoffmann–La Roche, Psychic Tension, The DSM, Hypnotherapy, Ketamine, The Maudsley Deprescribing Guidelines, A Small Matisse at the Met, Pruning Pills, Sensory Waterboarding, A Wedding, Another Drug, A New Self

In April of 2021, I walked into Toronto’s Centre for Addiction and Mental Health (CAMH). I had been feeling increasingly unstable, and despite not having a plan, my fantasies of suicide were getting harder to ignore. After unburdening myself to a triage nurse, I was ushered into a windowless room, relieved of my belt, and given paper slippers. The doctor who visited me said he thought I should stop taking Klonopin.

Examining my chart, he shook his head at my long-term, daily use. He said I shouldn’t have been taking Klonopin for so long, almost like I’d been writing my own prescriptions for the past nineteen years. Going off it, he told me, would reduce the mood swings that were making my life so difficult. I might briefly experience symptoms of withdrawal—increased blood pressure and heart rate, sweating, perhaps even tremors and seizures—and if I did, I should call 911. But it would be for the best, so I agreed. Six days later I was released with taper instructions intended to have me free of the drug in three weeks.

It took just two days on a smaller dose of Klonopin to feel profoundly uncomfortable. My hands were tingling, and I couldn’t stop sweating. I could still exercise, write, bathe, and cook meals. Within a week I could do none of those things. Here’s what happened to me as I tapered down to small doses of Klonopin, and then, for the first time since 2002, to none at all.

The tingling in my hands became numbness, which spread to my arms, legs, feet, and, briefly, my stomach. This is called paresthesia, which, combined with the sudden onset of stabbing pain and pressure in my neck, led to my first incorrect diagnosis, cervical radiculopathy, commonly called a pinched nerve. Tinnitus, a ringing in the ears—which I’d experienced before—­reappeared at shocking levels, like a million helium-fueled car alarms. I slept next to a speaker blaring white noise, although “slept” isn’t correct; I became an insomniac. Excessive sweating, hyperhidrosis, was the most embarrassing symptom. I packed spare shirts on the rare occasions when I left my apartment, and lost ten pounds. When I spoke aloud, my voice didn’t sound like mine, which is symptomatic of depersonalization. I became unspeakably sensitive to noise, light, and all things sensory. Then there was fasciculation: My left biceps began twitching, but this I welcomed, because now there was a symptom visible to my general practitioner—I wasn’t faking—although he still had no solution. I developed pain in both my hands, severe enough that I struggled to dress myself. This, along with a new, constant ache in my right knee, led to another misdiagnosis: arthritis. The first twenty minutes of each morning I spent vomiting, or retching, as I hardly ate. During the second week of withdrawal, I began to feel like a conduit for lightning, which I kept from my wife, Cristine, and from my general practitioner, because I worried I’d sound crazy. The sensation of being electrocuted for hours on end (and I don’t mean the “brain zaps” associated with SSRI withdrawal) was the most agonizing symptom. I’ve since learned that many people experience this during benzodiazepine withdrawal, and some end their lives because of it. My condition soon bridged mind and body and I became a tic person, compelled to bend my fingers in bizarre ways. The world smelled strange; I smelled strange. I didn’t know what was happening.

To say that these symptoms—and there were more; look up akathisia —exacerbated my “illness anxiety” would be a comic understatement. I knew that every hypochondriac is eventually vindicated, but that their “I told you so” has a fatal price. After decades spent scanning my body for abnormalities, I believed my time had come. Having kicked opiates cold turkey in the past, I felt nostalgic for three simple days of traditional nausea, sweatiness, and bone-deep ache. As the weeks progressed, doctors at CAMH enrolled me in therapy and made a number of other suggestions that didn’t feel like they addressed the gravity of what I was going through. My terror became constant. I was on fire but couldn’t be extinguished. I paced and cried and trembled and sweated. Although I suffered intensely from the physical effects of benzodiazepine withdrawal, I was broken by the emotions. I’d never been so anxious, and for the first time in my life, I was suicidal with a plan .

A couple of months after my stay at CAMH, I found a glimmer of hope. During a 12-step meeting, held on Zoom because of the pandemic, I shared that I’d been diagnosed with a pinched nerve and would potentially need surgery. I also mentioned that I’d recently been tapered off Klonopin. A person with their camera off sent me a message urging me not to have surgery. They suspected I had something called benzodiazepine withdrawal syndrome (BWS) and recommended I look up Dr. Heather Ashton.

After the meeting I did as suggested and discovered a number of websites run by medical professionals concerned about the effects of benzos, and an enormous online community of people like myself. They’d also been prescribed a benzodiazepine with assurances that it was safe, then dis­continued it, and were enduring what they often described as the worst experience of their lives. Their doctors were baffled, and sometimes accused them of lying. One doctor, however, was their patron saint: Heather Ashton, a British psychopharmacologist, who in 1999 published Benzodiazepines: How They Work and How to Withdraw , known colloquially as the Ashton Manual. It details every symptom I was experiencing, and outlines a frightening array of problems related to benzodiazepines.

Klonopin is one of numerous benzodiazepines regularly prescribed for anxiety and insomnia. Commonly called tranquilizers—brilliantly effective branding—the most well known of these central-nervous-system depressants are alprazolam, lorazepam, diazepam, and clonazepam (or Xanax, Ativan, Valium, and Klonopin, respectively). They are among the most widely prescribed medications in America. Today the safety of these medications is increasingly being questioned, but initially Dr. Ashton was just one of a handful of skeptics. Another, Professor Malcolm Lader from King’s College London, began sounding the alarm in the 1970s. In 1981, Lader warned of an “epidemic in the making,” and in 1999 he said, “It is more difficult to withdraw people from benzodiazepines than it is from heroin.” Nonetheless, according to the most recent study estimating total benzodiazepine use among Americans, which analyzed data from 2015 and 2016, an estimated 30.6 million American adults had taken benzodiazepines in the previous twelve months, with 25.3 million of them using them as prescribed.

In her manual—the most accessible of all benzodiazepine-awareness materials, and thus the one most suffering patients first discover—Ashton speculates that 10 to 15 percent of those taking benzos (potentially millions of Americans) will experience protracted withdrawal, as I did, and still do. Others, like Sean Hood, a researcher from the University of Western Australia’s School of Psychiatry and Clinical Neurosciences, believe it could be much more—up to 40 percent. Yet in medical school, students spend only a few hours studying benzodiazepines, perhaps a few more, depending on their residency. In 2020, after decades of mounting concerns, the FDA finally mandated a boxed warning for benzodiazepines indicating that “clinically significant physical dependence” was possible, as were “life-threatening” withdrawal reactions. Unfortunately, as Dr. Alexis Ritvo—an addiction psychiatrist in Colorado, and the medical director of the Alliance for Benzodiazepine Best Practices—explains, patients and their doctors aren’t necessarily aware of the warnings: “While the FDA publishes their boxed warnings, there is no formal way prescribers are required to be educated about them.”

Doctors at CAMH had assured me that benzodiazepines usually “clear the system” in two, perhaps three weeks—a commonly held belief—so any withdrawal symptoms would likely persist only that long. 1 Ashton and others believe that withdrawal can last months, even years. Days after I read Ashton’s manual, a specialist in Toronto said my “symptoms suggested multiple sclerosis,” four words that would terrify any hypochondriac, anxious, or ordinary person. I now know this misdiagnosis isn’t uncommon, as BWS can mimic the symptoms of MS, along with other illnesses and injuries.

According to Ashton and several recent studies, benzodiazepines alter brain function through neuroadaptation that persists after dis­continuation. Initially, they work by enhancing the effect of a neurotransmitter called gamma-­aminobutyric acid (GABA), the body’s tranquilizer. With long-term use, the brain adapts by reducing—downregulating—both the number and sensitivity of GABA receptors. At the same time, the brain’s excitatory neurotransmitter, glutamate, becomes more active without GABA’s soothing influence. Once someone discontinues a benzo, their GABA-suppressed brain, full of unchecked glutamate, creates a chronically hyperstimulated nervous system. GABA receptors eventually do upregulate—taking their own sweet time—and the brain resumes soothing itself, but until that happens, for some people, as for me, the physiological sense of being in danger is persistent, and debilitating. To paraphrase a post from the peer-­support site BenzoBuddies: If my nervous system is a car, benzo withdrawal has tied a brick to the gas pedal and disabled the brakes.

items.title: Alberta's decisive decision to stay in Canada gives Carney backing to take on Trump
items.summary: The overwhelming vote by Alberta to stay in Canada gives Mark Carney political capital to focus on remaking the country's economy, writes the BBC's Lyse Doucet.
items.content:
"Vote like Canada depends on it," Prime Minister Mark Carney declared to cheering crowds in Calgary last week on a stage emblazoned with bright red and white "Forever Canadian" banners.

It's a message that appears to have struck a chord with the electorate, as preliminary results show more than two-thirds of Alberta voters said they want to remain a part of Canada.

But the future of the federation does still rest on its richest province.

Alberta, with most of Canada's proven oil reserves and abundant gas and mineral wealth, is playing a pivotal role in Ottawa's drive to survive a punishing trade war with the US by diversifying trade, strengthening its economy, and forging new alliances on the other side of the world.

Carney, the former central banker who grew up in Alberta, is now Canada's builder-in-chief – at home, and beyond its borders.

Note the emphasis in his first statement after Monday's vote on separation in the province, as soon as the scale of the victory was clear: "They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other."

Albertans' overwhelming "yes" to stay in Canada gives him political bricks and mortar, too.

"Don't mess with Canada," warned Thomas Lukaszuk, a former lawmaker whose Forever Canadian campaign played a key role in this referendum's outcome.

Addressing elated supporters in Edmonton, the provincial capital, as the "yes" count for Canada kept tumbling in, Lukaszuk underlined that this vote "will send a very strong message to the rest of the world".

Everyone knows he's talking about the troublesome neighbour to the south – in particular its president, who keeps threatening to turn Canada into the 51st US state.

The same day Albertans were voting on their future in Canada, Trump sent his own signal north at a rally in Kansas ahead of next month's US midterm polls.

"I will let you keep ice hockey, and I will let you keep your 'O Canada' national anthem," he promised before adding: "We're only kidding."

In the run up to this referendum, Carney reiterated a warning he's often sounded that "there are some outside our borders who are working to break us, so they own us" – even if he didn't spell out who "they" is.

And, in this defining time for the separatist camp, some in their ranks didn't hide their direction of travel. Some of their most prominent leaders admitted they travelled to Washington three times last year to meet US State Department officials and outline what an independent Alberta could offer – including a possible oil pipeline through the US to the Pacific.

But the rest of the world may take only passing notice of what was, for Canada, an historic vote sparking conversations and concerns across the country, from coast to coast to coast.

"Short of a vote to separate, most foreign governments, with the exception of the United States, have little interest in domestic Canadian politics," says Professor Janice Stein, founding director of the Munk School of Global Affairs and Public Policy at the University of Toronto.

"Foreign investors are focused on the time it will take to complete major infrastructure projects, a return on investment, and predictable regulations," she explains in a nod to Carney's long list of megaprojects he hopes will eventually turbocharge economic growth. They're all costly; many will take years to build.

An ambitious blueprint already includes a proposed pipeline to the Pacific coast which opens opportunities for Alberta's oil to reach Asian markets – a move which also addresses Alberta's long-standing grievance that its economy has been stifled by federal policies, including environmental regulations.

At a rally in Alberta last week, it was Carney's comment that the pipeline "will reduce our dependence on the United States" that triggered the loudest and longest applause of the night.

After Monday's vote, Carney – the former UN Special Envoy for Climate Action and Finance – pointed to "unleashing our full potential as a global energy superpower with Alberta as its core". Political and economic pressures now seem to eclipse his green credentials.

'Great result for Canada', says Carney as Alberta votes to reject separatism

Huge setback for Alberta's separatist movement after decisive defeat

"Build Canada Strong" has been Carney's mantra ever since he first entered politics, a complete neophyte, at the start of last year.

At home there are possible wide-reaching repercussions from the final tallies in the referendum's nine other questions which dealt with issues ranging from greater provincial powers, the costs of immigration, and potential constitutional changes.

Those results are certain to provoke debate, and deal making or breaking, involving Canada's nine other provinces and three territories. They all have their own grievances, too.

The prime minister has had to defend himself when journalists ask if he is spending too much time on foreign trips with his charm offensive to build new political alliances and trade partnerships, including an unprecedented and still uncertain offer of associate membership of the European Union.

"I can do both and I need to do both," he recently replied with his signature bluntness before listing the more than 16 bills which went through Parliament in the last session dealing with everything from major tax changes, public safety, and the price of fuel.

For now, Carney is riding high in the polls at home – including in Alberta, which doesn't traditionally support his Liberal party - in a long "political honeymoon" other beleaguered politicians would envy.

And the plain-speaking politician's strong and steady response to Trump threats, including retaliatory tariffs, has seen his star rising on the world stage. It's an unexpected turn for a country which has often been missing from top tables and has sometimes even been dismissed as "boring".

The Economist magazine decided to put Carney on their cover, on this week of weeks for Canada, with a perfect red maple leaf between his teeth.

"Mark Carney shows middle powers how to handle a dangerous world," reads one of its headlines, with an article which also focuses on Canada's "vulnerabilities" including Alberta's ballot.

"The broader takeaway from this vote might be that Canadian unity is in fine shape," remarks David Moscrop, political scientist and author of the forthcoming book On Nationalism.

"But what happens after Donald Trump is gone and Canada no longer has a single, bombastic target which drives Canadians to rally around the flag?" he asks.

Carney's decision to recently walk away from trade talks with the US gave rise to another swell of Canadian pride and patriotism. But if this trade war drags on with a country which traditionally takes 70% of Canada's exports, Canadians will feel even greater pain in their daily lives.

"It's a win for Team Canada and its resilience," commented CBC journalist Janyce McGregor during the public broadcaster's rolling coverage.

items.title: Feds suspect ransom negotiator ran ShinyHunters extortion site
items.summary: Article URL: https://krebsonsecurity.com/2026/10/feds-suspect-ransom-negotiator-ran-shinyhunters-extortion-site/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50173487 Points: 223 # Comments: 109
items.content:
U.S. federal investigators pursuing the ShinyHunters hacking group that recently stole highly sensitive data from the FBI have identified executives at two different ransomware negotiation firms who maintained unusually close relations with the extortion group, KrebsOnSecurity has learned. Sources close to the investigation say one of the executives in the United States even helped ShinyHunters operate a website that pressured victims into paying a ransom.

Hackers aligned with ShinyHunters have claimed credit for dozens of major data breaches since 2019, when the group was primarily operated by cybercriminals living in France. As those original members were arrested or jailed one by one, control over the ShinyHunters brand eventually passed to “ Rey ,” identified last year as a teenage hacker from Amman, Jordan. According to the FBI, ShinyHunters has extorted more than $70 million from victims so far this year.

In late September, ShinyHunters hacked the FBI recruitment website fbijobs.gov and taunted the agency by threatening to publish the stolen files, which reportedly included medical and psychological records, Social Security numbers and home addresses, and information about each employee’s unit and specialization.

The FBI jobs site hack has prompted the agency to move with uncommon speed to arrest, detain and question people who had any communications with Rey or other ShinyHunters suspects. Reuters reported on October 3 that Rey had been detained by Jordanian authorities and was cooperating with the FBI.

Rey was able to assume control over the hacking group because one of its alleged senior members had just been nabbed. On the evening of September 15, 2026, authorities in the Netherlands arrested convicted hacker and ShinyHunters suspect Pepijn van der Stap . Dutch police reportedly used flash-bang grenades in an effort to stun and apprehend Van der Stap as he was logged in to various online accounts.

According to a source close to the investigation, the authorities arrested Van der Stap while he was using his Signal instant messaging account, which allowed them to read recent communications with frequent contacts — including ransomware negotiators based in Canada and the United States.

Multiple sources with knowledge of the matter told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s messages were the key to unraveling a murder-for-hire plot that emerged immediately following his arrest. The Dutch news outlet RTL reported last month the two murders were allegedly to be committed abroad, and that there are indications Van der Stap gave the order for the attacks (there is no indication those orders were ever carried out).

On October 9, KrebsOnSecurity broke the news that the FBI arrested a 54-year-old Canadian cybersecurity executive named Edward Dubrovsky in connection with the ShinyHunters investigation. Dubrovsky, who recently published a book on handling cyber extortion that recommended always engaging with the hackers, was charged with threatening to disclose stolen or hacked data and interfering with interstate commerce through extortion, according to court records . Politico reports prosecutors have asked that Dubrovsky remain in custody pending trial, and that records related to his case remain under seal.

A source close to the investigation told KrebsOnSecurity that Van der Stap’s Signal messages showed he had frequent conversations with Mr. Dubrovsky and with at least one executive at a large U.S.-based consulting firm, and that these executives often knew the details about new ShinyHunters victims before the victims themselves had even learned of the breach.

That source shared another potentially explosive finding by federal investigators: the Dutch hacker’s chats showed Mr. Dubrovsky knew ShinyHunters had stolen highly sensitive data from FBI servers, and that he never informed the bureau of the data breach prior to ShinyHunters threatening on Twitter/X to publish the agency’s deeply personal personnel files.

KrebsOnSecurity has learned from two sources close to the ShinyHunters probe that FBI investigators believe at least one executive at a U.S.-based consulting firm played an active role in operating the now-defunct ShinyHunters victim extortion website “ shinywire[.]com .” KrebsOnSecurity is not naming the U.S. company or the suspected executive(s) for now because they have not yet been charged with a crime, but it is a prestigious firm with more than 1,000 associates.

A section of the homepage for the now-defunct Shinywire website.

The Shinywire website was active from approximately May 3, 2026 until October 16 and had entries for nearly 100 organizations hacked by ShinyHunters. Each entry urged victims to engage with the cybercrime group and discuss terms for payment. The pages also included samples of stolen files and promised those files would be published online if the victim ignored their demands.

The following screenshot shows a cached portion of the Shinywire extortion page for Intuitive Surgical , an American medical technology company that was breached in March 2026 after an employee fell for a targeted phishing email.

The Shinywire website, as indexed by urlscan.io. This listing is an extortion demand targeting Intuitive Surgical, an American medical technology company breached in March 2026 by a targeted phishing email attack that compromised an employee’s credentials.

Victim organizations that refused to engage or negotiate after seven days would find all of their stolen data published on the ShinyHunters victim shaming blog (a website that is only reachable via the anonymity network Tor ).

In a story published October 15, The Globe and Mail wrote that a few months before Edward Dubrovsky was arrested by the FBI, the Canadian cybersecurity executive alleged in court documents he had become collateral damage in a campaign by a former business partner to “destroy” another industry executive.

The story noted that Dubrovsky filed the lawsuit in Ontario this year against Daniel Tobok , the former chief executive of Cypfer , a cybersecurity firm founded in Toronto with offices in the U.S., Britain, the Netherlands, the United Arab Emirates, and Mexico. The two first became business partners in 2017 and later developed Cypfer together, where Mr. Dubrovsky was a managing partner and chief operating officer. But by 2024, the two had a falling out, with Dubrovsky accusing Tobok of gradually excluding him from business matters and making “increasingly capricious business decisions.”

Mr. Tobok reportedly denied the allegations and filed a counterclaim, accusing Mr. Dubrovsky of accessing confidential information and unfairly competing with Cypfer through work at another firm called CyberSteward Inc . He also said Mr. Dubrovsky has misrepresented himself as a Cypfer founder, and is not a shareholder.

According to interviews with several former colleagues of Mr. Tobok, as far back as eight years ago he was known to ransomware purveyors by a particular nickname: Ghostbyte . In 2018, a Canadian company was hacked by Dharma , a prolific Russian-language ransomware affiliate program that first surfaced in 2016. The victim company told the Dharma ransomware representative they were leaning toward paying because some of the files were unrecoverable after being locked, but that they needed a better guarantee that Dharma would keep their word if paid.

A redacted copy of the Dharma rep’s reply is pictured below, and it shows the ransomware group urged the victim to contact a person at a Canadian IT firm that helps companies seeking such guarantees. The Dharma rep recommended the victim contact the email address ghostbyte@tutanota.com .

“If you want guarantees, you can write to the IT company,” the Dharma reply advised. “Take the phone and negotiate with them. This IT company often solves such problems in Canada. You can contact them and sign a contract for services. You’ll still have to pay.”

An email reply from the Dharma ransomware group to a victim, recommending they contact an email address that is connected to Mr. Tobok.

It’s unclear if Mr. Tobok ever used that Ghostbyte address offered by the Dharma representative, and he has not responded to multiple requests for comment. However, the breach tracking service Constella Intelligence finds an email address Mr. Tobok has frequently used — dtobok@me.com — is associated with two online accounts where the chosen username was “ghostbyte,” including a Snapchat account.

Incidentally, Constella also finds the Dharma rep’s email address luckygoodlucky@tuta.io is associated with a cryptocurrency address that processed 38 transactions totaling 43 bitcoin, ~$3.5 million at today’s value (the most recent transaction for this wallet is dated February 2019).

In a statement shared on October 14, Cypfer said the company’s business does not include making or facilitating ransomware payments, and that Cypfer learned of Dubrovsky’s arrest when the news first broke in the media.

“We had no prior knowledge of Mr. Dubrovsky’s arrest,” a spokesperson told KrebsOnSecurity via email. “ CYPFER has not received any outreach from law enforcement and, to our knowledge, is not the target of any law enforcement investigation.”

items.title: Guerra in Iran, news. Ft: “Netanyahu voleva attaccare l’Iran il 10 ottobre, Trump ha detto no”
items.summary: Media: “Don Jr rompe con Trump sulla guerra in Iran” . Rubio: “Difficile raggiungere un accordo”. Londra invia caccia Raf in Arabia Saudita contro gli Houthi
items.content:
Il premier israeliano Benjamin Netanyahu sta spingendo per la ripresa di attacchi su larga scala contro l'Iran e all'inizio di questo mese aveva incaricato le sue forze armate di pianificare una nuova offensiva di vasta portata. Lo scrive il Financial Times . Secondo tre persone a conoscenza dei fatti, l'esercito israeliano si era preparato per una campagna di bombardamenti di più giorni, prevista per il fine settimana del 10 ottobre, che avrebbe preso di mira infrastrutture civili come centrali elettriche, impianti nucleari e obiettivi del regime.

La missione alla fine non è andata avanti, e le fonti vicine alla vicenda hanno citato l'opposizione del presidente Donald Trump alla ripresa del conflitto prima delle elezioni di medio termine statunitensi del 3 novembre.

Jerusalem Post: “Idf non aveva in programma un attacco all'Iran il 10 ottobre”

Macron: “Al lavoro con l'Italia per una forza multinazionale a sostegno del Libano”

Media, Israele vieta a pilota United Airlines di entrare nello spazio aereo del Paese

Ft: “Netanyahu era pronto ad attaccare l'Iran il 10 ottobre, Trump ha detto no”

Jerusalem Post: “Idf non aveva in programma un attacco all'Iran il 10 ottobre”

Contrariamente alle notizie riferite dal Financial Times, l'Idf non aveva in programma un attacco contro l'Iran per il 10 ottobre, secondo fonti del Jerusalem Post. Né il primo ministro Benjamin Netanyahu, né il ministro della Difesa Israel Katz, né alcun altro funzionario governativo, avevano ordinato all'Idf di prepararsi all'attacco. "Quindi - hanno detto le fonti - la premessa di Ft - secondo cui Trump avrebbe impedito a Israele di attaccare l'Iran, è errata, perché Israele non aveva alcuna intenzione di attaccare".

Macron: “Al lavoro con l'Italia per una forza multinazionale a sostegno del Libano”

"Deploriamo la decisione di porre fine al mandato" della forza multinazionale Unifil che operava da decenni in sostegno all'esercito libanese. "Penso che il presidente Joseph Aoun, andando a Washington, si aspettasse di ottenere una garanzia americana per un proseguimento. Peccato che il suo auspicio non sia stato accolto, penso sia un errore. Lavoriamo con l'Italia ed altri partner ad altre forze multinazionali, nella speranza che possano avere un mandato delle Nazioni Unite ed un sostegno chiaro": lo ha detto il presidente francese, Emmanuel Macron rispondendo ai cronisti a Doha, in Qatar, ultima tappa della sua missione in Medio Oriente. La Francia, ha proseguito il leader d'Oltralpe, "è pronta a contribuirvi, per un sostegno alle forze libanesi, e in un quadro chiaro e ordinato di ritiro delle forze israeliane dal Libano meridionale.

Candidato al Congresso Usa su X: “Fermato da Idf in Cisgiordania, raccoglievo olive”

Brad Lander, candidato ebreo democratico al Congresso degli Stati Uniti, ha annunciato in un post su X di "essere stato fermato dall'Idf, insieme a un gruppo di rabbini e volontari". "Stavamo semplicemente raccogliendo olive in un uliveto vicino a Nehalim, in Cisgiordania. L'occupazione è un crimine secondo il diritto internazionale. Raccogliere olive non è un reato secondo nessuna legge che io conosca", ha scritto. L'organizzazione 'Rabbini per i Diritti Umani' ha reso noto che l'Idf ha arrestato circa 80 volontari dell'organizzazione e attivisti americani che stavano accompagnando dei contadini palestinesi durante la raccolta delle olive nel villaggio di Nahalin, nella zona di Betlemme. Secondo l'organizzazione, i volontari sono arrivati sul posto nelle prime ore del mattino e, dopo circa due ore di lavoro nei campi, le forze dell'Idf sono giunte sul posto e hanno notificato un ordine di zona militare chiusa valido per 24 ore. Sempre secondo l'organizzazione, i rappresentanti hanno informato i militari che avrebbero rispettato l'ordine e avrebbero evacuato l'area, ma i soldati hanno fermato tutti per identificarli e hanno fotografato i documenti d'identità e i passaporti di ciascuno. Tra gli attivisti anche Brad Lander, candidato al Congresso di New York.

Pasdaran: “Cavi sottomarini a Hormuz nel mirino se Usa attaccano nostre infrastrutture”

I Guardiani della Rivoluzione, i Pasdaran iraniani, minacciano di prendere di mira i cavi sottomarini in caso di raid contro le infrastrutture della Repubblica islamica. "Se (Usa e alleati) dovessero tentare di danneggiare le nostre infrastrutture, la Repubblica islamica utilizzerebbe naturalmente tutta la sua potenza - ha affermato Yadollah Javani, generale dei Pasdaran, in dichiarazioni all'emittente iraniana Al-Alam rilanciate dalla tv satellitare al-Jazeera - La Repubblica islamica può distruggere facilmente i loro asset, compresi i sette importanti cavi da cui transita il traffico Internet sotto le acque dello Stretto di Hormuz". L'Iran, ha minacciato, è in grado di "infliggere danni molto gravi agli Usa e ai loro alleati nella regione". Nei giorni scorsi l'Iran aveva minacciato la distruzione di data center per l'intelligenza artificiale e cavi sottomarini se dovessero riprendere i raid contro la Repubblica islamica. Teheran "non ha ancora giocato tutte le sue carte", diceva il capo del Consiglio per la sicurezza nazionale dell'Iran, Mohsen Rezaei.

Coalizione saudita: “Duri scontri con gli Houthi nel sud-ovest yemenita”

La coalizione a guida saudita afferma che le sue forze sono impegnate in pesanti combattimenti contro gli Houthi a Kahboub, nel sud-ovest dello Yemen, e stanno cercando di respingere un attacco su larga scala da parte del gruppo sostenuto dall'Iran. Lo afferma Al-Jazeera.

Putin a Witkoff: “Pronti a contribuire a risoluzione della crisi iraniana”

La Russia è pronta a contribuire alla risoluzione della crisi iraniana. Lo ha sottolineato il presidente russo, Vladimir Putin, durante l'incontro a San Pietroburgo con l'inviato statunitense, Steve Witkoff, secondo quanto riferito dall'agenzia Tass. "Se possiamo fare qualcosa per risolvere questa crisi, saremo lieti di farlo", ha affermato Putin, sottolineando che Mosca intrattiene con Teheran "un rapporto speciale e di fiducia", consolidato nel corso di decenni.

Media, Israele vieta a pilota United Airlines di entrare nello spazio aereo del Paese

Il ministero dei Trasporti ha ufficialmente vietato a un pilota della compagnia aerea United Airlines di entrare nello spazio aereo israeliano. Lo riferisce l'emittente Channel 12. Il pilota, Sina Amjadjan, di origine iraniana, è dipendente della compagnia e risiede a Dubai. Secondo quanto riportato sui social network, avrebbe espresso sostegno al regime iraniano, ai Guardiani della Rivoluzione e all'organizzazione terroristica Hezbollah. Le informazioni su Amjadjan sono state trasmesse dal ministero per gli Affari della Diaspora al ministero dei Trasporti dopo un'attività di monitoraggio avviata in seguito all'incidente sul volo della Flydubai.

Iran: “Le minacce ripetute ci portano ad avere una difesa più efficace”

Il ministro della Difesa iraniano, Mehrdad Akhlaghi, ha dichiarato che la Repubblica islamica sta aumentando la sua preparazione militare per rispondere a minacce. "Per noi, rispondere a minacce ripetute non è una gara di retorica. Significa trasformare tali minacce in una maggiore prontezza e in capacità difensive più efficaci", ha detto Akhlaghi, che nelle scorse settimane è stato nominato nuovo ministro della Difesa di Teheran e pochi giorni fa ha ufficialmente ricevuto l'incarico dopo l'approvazione da parte del Parlamento. "Sosterremo qualunque sforzo, ma non rinunceremo alla nostra terra", ha aggiunto il funzionario in un messaggio su X, come riferisce Iran International, sottolineando che una delle sue priorità immediate in quanto ministro della Difesa sarà soddisfare le esigenze della Forza aerospaziale dei Guardiani della Rivoluzione e della componente di difesa aerea delle forze armate regolari.

Una petroliera è stata colpita da "munizioni non identificate" a circa 20 chilometri a ovest della città di Bukha, in Oman. Lo ha reso noto l'Agenzia britannica per le operazioni marittime (Ukmto), aggiungendo che dopo l'attacco è scoppiato un incendio successivamente domato e che la petroliera è ancorata. L'agenzia ha inoltre riferito che nessun membro dell'equipaggio è rimasto ferito.

Iran: nave colpita da proiettile sconosciuto nello Stretto di Hormuz

Una nave è stata colpita da un proiettile di origine sconosciuta al largo delle coste dell'Oman, vicino allo Stretto di Hormuz. Lo riferisce l'agenzia britannica per la sicurezza marittima Ukmto, secondo la quale l'attacco ha provocato un incendio che è stato domato. La petroliera, che si trovava a 11 miglia nautiche (circa 20 chilometri) a ovest della città di Bukha, è "attualmente all'ancora. Tutti i membri dell'equipaggio sono al sicuro e finora non si segnalano impatti ambientali", ha dichiarato l'agenzia.

Houthi: “Colpita la sala operativa saudita del campo militare di Aden”

"Le nostre forze armate sono riuscite a colpire con un missile balistico la sala operativa del nemico saudita nel campo militare di Badr ad Aden, e il colpo è stato preciso e diretto". Lo scrive su X il portavoce militare degli Houthi Yahya Saree.

items.title: Rivolte in Francia e Italia: due Paesi per vecchi che si sono dimenticati dei loro giovani
items.summary: Outlook del 21 ottobre. Iscriviti alla Newsletter
items.content:
Benvenuti su Outlook, la newsletter di Repubblica che analizza l'economia, la finanza, i mercati internazionali. Ogni mercoledì parleremo di società quotate e no, di personaggi, istituzioni, di scandali e inchieste legate a questo mondo. Se volete scrivermi, la mia mail è w.galbiati@repubblica.it.

Vetrine spaccate, saccheggi, auto e cassonetti messi a fuoco. Scenari da guerriglia urbana che hanno visto fronteggiarsi poliziotti in assetto anti-sommossa contro giovani e giovanissimi. La rabbia è esplosa in Francia , ma ha trovato eco anche in altri Paesi, compresa l’ Italia .

Il disagio si è prima concretizzato in manifestazioni organizzate da studenti, ma poi è diventato guerriglia urbana , pura rabbia alimentata dai social, senza punti di riferimento se non quello di distruggere e saccheggiare .

Le crisi . Le razzie sono lo specchio dei fallimenti politici che sia in Francia che in Italia hanno inanellato le ultime legislature , crisi esasperate dal caro vita , innescato dall’attacco Usa all’Iran.

1) Il caso francese . La Francia ha visto crescere a dismisura il proprio debito , salito in sei anni di mille miliardi e arrivato al 120% del Pil . Pur essendo uno dei Paesi che più investe nel sociale , ha ora le mani legate per intervenire là dove servirebbe, come nel campo della scuola e della formazione .

I benefici . Investire nell’ istruzione significa credere nella sua dimensione sociale e nella capacità che ha di generare valore per i giovani e il futuro del Paese . Certo, non può essere tutto, ma, oltre che inclusione, la scuola può creare mobilità sociale e ridurre le disuguaglianze che oggi muovono buona parte delle proteste .

Casse vuote. In molti Paesi europei, mancano nuovi fondi e con le elezioni in arrivo, si bada più a soddisfare gli interessi dei potenziali bacini elettorali che altro.

In Francia la spesa è al 57% del Pil e gli interessi sul debito, con i rendimenti dei titoli decennali superiori a quelli dell’Italia, si mangiano lo spazio di manovra all’interno del bilancio pubblico.

Il deficit sfora il 5% , non una novità perché negli ultimi 31 anni Parigi ha avuto disavanzi per 28 esercizi , con l’ultimo saldo positivo che risale al lontano 2001.

Molte spese per i vecchi . Quel che non torna è che le spese non sono indirizzate per creare un futuro ai giovani e nemmeno a garantire un patto intergenerazionale .

Lo Stato utilizza un quarto del suo bilancio per pagare le pensioni , che pesano intorno al 15% del Pil , quando la media dei Paesi Ocse si ferma al 9,1% e dei Paesi Ue al 13%.

Si tratta di una incidenza che è cresciuta ininterrottamente dal 2000 (era intorno al 12% del Pil ) andando a gonfiare la spesa per la protezione sociale . Una tendenza che mostra come la bilancia non penda a favore dei più giovani.

Anche l’ultima riforma delle pensioni voluta dal presidente Macron che avrebbe dovuto togliere qualche privilegio innalzando l’età pensionabile da 62 a 64 anni è stata subito congelata e non entrerà in funzione prima del 2028 .

Sempre che non vadano al potere Le Pen (Rassemblement National) o Jean-Luc Mélenchon (La France Insoumise) che hanno già annunciato di volerla bloccare.

Poche spese per i giovani . Dal 2000 a oggi, la spesa per l’istruzione francese non solo non è cresciuta , rimanendo costante tra i 5 e il 6% del Pil , ma secondo l’Ocse, restringendo il periodo di osservazione, si sta ridimensionando per importanza .

Nei Paesi monitorati dall’Ocse, tra il 2015 e il 2023 la spesa pubblica per l’istruzione è infatti diminuita in termini relativi , passando dal 10,9% dei bilanci pubblici al 10,1% .

In Francia non è andata diversamente: la spesa pro capite per studente è aumentata da 13.898 a 14.794 dollari , ma la quota destinata all’istruzione è scesa dall’ 8,3% dei bilanci pubblici all’ 8,0% .

Le scuole a pezzi . In difficoltà sono anche le strutture e il corpo insegnanti . In Francia le proteste sono partite dal liceo Paul Éluard di Saint-Denis , una delle periferie più povere di Parigi , dove gli studenti hanno documentato la presenza di topi e scarafaggi , nonché la fatiscenza della struttura, assediata da infiltrazioni d’acqua e con soffitti cadenti .

Il Paul Éluard , inaugurato nel 1965 , ha 61 anni di età , ma la categoria a cui appartiene, i licei polivalenti non è nemmeno la peggiore in Francia perché queste strutture hanno un’ età media di 44 anni .

Gli edifici dei licei professionali , dei licei di istruzione generale e tecnologica e delle scuole medie se la passano decisamente peggio : hanno le costruzioni più antiche di tutti con in media rispettivamente 71, 65 e 61 anni di età .

Le ristrutturazioni , poi, sono qualcosa di raro, perché non sono in capo allo Stato, ma alle amministrazioni locali che hanno ovviamente meno capacità di spesa .

Gli insegnanti sottopagati... Il secondo problema riguarda gli insegnanti che si sono uniti alla protesta degli studenti . In ogni parte del mondo, i docenti hanno stipendi più bassi rispetto a quelli di altri lavoratori con lo stesso livello di istruzione .

Ciò vale anche in Francia: chi insegna nella scuola secondaria di primo grado guadagna in media il 10% in meno rispetto a chi è in possesso di uno stesso titolo di studio universitario, una percentuale che peggiora per gli inseganti della scuola di infanzia il cui stipendio è inferiore del 18% .

Negli ultimi dieci anni le paghe non sono cresciute e, secondo i dati Ocse, solo il 26,6% del corpo docente della scuola secondaria di primo grado francese si dichiara soddisfatto di quanto riceve a fine mese .

… e anziani . In più gli insegnanti tendono ad avere anche un’età più avanzata rispetto agli altri lavoratori: il 23% di chi è impiegato nella scuola secondaria ha 55 anni o più , rispetto al 20% della popolazione attiva complessiva. Non favorendo l’aggiornamento e la vicinanza ai giovani .

A tutto ciò si aggiungono le carenze di organico . Nel 2025 , quasi il 10% delle ore di insegnamento non sono state coperte , per lo più per la mancanza di docenti . E continuano ad aumentare le assenze di professori senza una sostituzione.

Il caso Italia. Non molto diversa è la situazione in Italia . I conti sono sotto pressione con il debito fermo al 138,4% del Pil , lo stesso rapporto di quando si è insediato il governo Meloni cinque anni fa, ma con una crescita di 600 miliardi in valore assoluto.

Il peso del debito . Gli interessi si mangiano il 4,3% del Pil e non consentono di incrementare la spesa per istruzione , nonostante l’Italia, a differenza della Francia, abbia avuto avanzi primari in 26 degli ultimi 31 esercizi di bilancio .

Siamo anche noi un Paese per vecchi non solo perché nascono meno bambini e aumentano gli anziani, ma perché le spese pubbliche , come quelle francesi vanno soprattutto in questa direzione .

Le pensioni . Ai pensionati finisce il 16% del Pil , una incidenza seconda solo a quella della Grecia in ambito Ocse. Un aggravio sul bilancio elevato, tanto più che un quarto delle spesa previdenziale non è finanziato dai contributi pensionistici, ma pesca direttamente dalle altre tasse .

La Riforma Dini . Nel 1995 per mitigarne l’effetto sui conti, la Riforma Dini ha introdotto il regime pensionistico contributivo , ma l’attuazione sotto la spinta degli interessi elettorali dei partiti è stata sempre rallentata e peggiorata dalle varie “quote” ,i pensionamenti anticipati.

Solo dal 2040 ci sarà la piena attuazione con il risultato che fino ad allora la spesa pensionistica continuerà a essere un fardello per le finanze pubbliche.

Sanità e assistenza . Il conto si aggrava ulteriormente se alle pensioni si aggiungono i costi della sanità e per la cura e l’ assistenza delle persone anziane .

Sommando queste componenti, nel 2025 si è arrivati al 22,5% del Pil che salirà al 25,5% nel 2043 , soprattutto per via della spesa pensionistica che toccherà il suo picco nel 2038 al 17,1% del Pil.

La scuola . Sul fronte dell’istruzione, l’ Italia fa peggio della Francia . Vi investe solo il 4% del Pil , circa 88 miliardi di euro , che sono più o meno gli stessi soldi pagati per gli interessi sul debito.

Fanalini di coda . Sono numeri che pongono il Paese al di sotto della media Ue pari al 4,7% del Pil . Tra il 2015 e il 2022 in Italia, la spesa pro-capite per studente è sì aumentata da 11.731 a 12.493 dollari , ma la quota destinata all’istruzione è scesa dal 7,1% dei bilanci pubblici al 6,7% , seguendo lo stesso trend della Francia e di tutti i Paesi Ocse .

Le conseguenze . I minori investimenti si fanno sentire sul tessuto sociale. Le persone con un livello di istruzione più elevato finiscono più difficilmente tra i senza lavoro e percepiscono salari più elevati .

In Italia il 14,8% dei giovani adulti economicamente attivi (di età compresa tra i 25 e i 34 anni ) privi di un titolo di istruzione secondaria superiore è disoccupato , una incidenza peggiore rispetto agli altri Paesi Ocse la cui media si ferma al 12,9% .

E sempre in Italia chi non ha un titolo di studio secondario percepisce il 19% in meno di chi ne è in possesso ( 17% la media Ocse ).

items.title: Suspect arrested after historic town hall set alight - French media
items.summary: The spire of the clock tower at Limoges city hall dramatically collapsed as it was engulfed in flames on Saturday.
items.content:
A suspect linked to a far-left movement has been arrested in France after a 19th Century city hall was gutted by a fire over the weekend that broke out during mass disorder, French media report.

The clock tower and parts of the roof of the ornate city hall in the central city of Limoges were engulfed in flames before collapsing on Saturday.

The 34-year-old suspect is known to police for acts of violence against public officials and is on a French national security watchlist, FranceInfo and BFM TV report.

French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu has vowed a "massive" police presence during further protests planned for Saturday, while several cities, including parts of Paris, will be subject to curfews this week.

Marseille mayor Benoît Payan said on X that the prefect had decided to introduce the curfew "starting this evening and for days to come", with French media reporting it would be in place overnight from Tuesday to Friday.

Payan said the measures apply to minors and will only be in commercial areas of the city, which were particularly affected by looting which took place last weekend.

Paris's police commissioner has also ordered the extension of an overnight curfew in the capital. The Préfecture de Police said the measure would continue "for as long as it proves necessary".

A curfew for parts of central Lyon was renewed on Tuesday, while overnight curfews for Nice and Lille are ongoing, and a week-long, overnight curfew for Bordeaux came into force on Tuesday night.

French Justice Minister Gérald Darmanin told BFM Television that 149 people were in detention following widespread demonstrations over the weekend.

Hundreds of thousands of demonstrators took to the streets to protest against rising fuel prices, the cost of living and deteriorating public services, including schools.

Darmanin previously said he asked prosecutors to be "extremely firm" and "ruthless towards those who attacked police officers, gendarmes and firefighters, who looted shops and who attacked public buildings".

Lecornu told French parliament on Tuesday afternoon a large number of police would meet demonstrators at a planned protest on Saturday.

Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez previously admitted police had "lost control" in some cities over the weekend.

He was strongly criticised by opposition politicians over authorities' preparedness for the disorder, leading him to offer his resignation on Monday, which was rejected by President Emmanuel Macron.

Lecornu also accused far-left groups of an "insurrectionary" plan over the weekend's mass chaos.

Responding to an earlier, similar accusation from Lecornu, left-wing La France Insoumise (LFI) de facto leader Jean-Luc Mélenchon had called for the prime minister to "prove his accusation" or "apologise, shut up, and stop stoking disorder".

On Tuesday, Mélenchon urged followers on social media to show "restraint" in the face of any "provocation".

Lecornu earlier said targeted curfews introduced across France on Monday contributed to a quiet night following the disorder.

Curfews were introduced across parts of central Paris, including Place de la République, where protesters had gathered over the weekend, and the Les Halles shopping area.

Other measures restricting the movement of young people and gatherings were introduced on Monday in cities such as Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south, as well as Lille and other towns in the north.

A crowd assembled in Lyon on Monday night in support of businesses affected by the disorder but dispersed without violating the curfew, officials said.

The Rhône prefecture said on social media that it was "furious" that a far-right group tried to hijack the gathering. The prefecture said on X it reported the group to the public prosecutor for alleged Islamophobic and xenophobic remarks.

Lecornu thanked police officers and gendarmes for enforcing the measures, adding that further curfews on Tuesday night would be decided depending on where they were necessary.

Writing in a post on X, he said decisions would be made "on the ground" by French regions and local mayors.

More than 2,500 people have been arrested since the disorder broke out, officials said on Monday. One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to the AFP news agency. About 1,000 police officers were injured.

Protests first began last month with students demanding better school conditions but they have escalated to take in a broader range of concerns with numbers at demonstrations bolstered by trade unions and various protest groups.

More than 2,000 shops and other businesses have been directly impacted by the weekend's violence, the head of France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.

Rioters, some dressed in black and wearing masks and balaclavas, were seen setting fire to cars and buildings and looting businesses in Paris, Marseille and other cities and smaller towns.

Protest organisers earlier declared that a second round of protests will take place on Saturday across France.

The so-called yellow vests (gilets jaunes), who were responsible for France's longest-ever modern protests in 2018, has said "Act II" will take place this weekend.

Meanwhile, French union La CGT has called for a major day of strikes on 5 November.

items.title: La Nigeria ha segnalato il primo caso di ebola dopo 12 anni: è legato all’epidemia partita dalla Repubblica Democratica del Congo
items.content:
Il ministro della Salute nigeriano Muhammad Ali Pate ha detto che nel paese è stato confermato il primo caso di ebola da quando la Nigeria era riuscita a estinguere la sua ultima epidemia nel 2014. La persona a cui è stata diagnosticata l’infezione è una donna che nelle scorse settimane aveva viaggiato in Uganda e poi era tornata ad Abuja, la capitale della Nigeria. Al momento si trova in isolamento in ospedale e il governo nigeriano ha detto di aver identificato 44 contatti stretti della donna.

La Nigeria è il primo paese dell’Africa occidentale a segnalare un caso legato all’epidemia di ebola che va avanti da mesi in Africa centrorientale e che era partita a maggio dalla Repubblica Democratica del Congo , dove sono morte più di 4.600 persone su oltre 9.500 casi: è la peggiore epidemia di ebola della storia del paese. Oltre alla Repubblica Democratica del Congo, negli scorsi mesi alcuni focolai più circoscritti sono stati segnalati anche in Kenya e in Uganda, che però a luglio aveva detto di non avere più casi.

Il virus dell’ebola si diffonde tramite il contatto con i fluidi corporei di persone infette, vive o morte. La malattia causa febbre, vomito, diarrea, e nei casi più gravi emorragie interne ed esterne. L’epidemia in corso attualmente è causata da virus della specie Bundibugyo ebolavirus , che storicamente è poco diffusa e quindi è stata meno studiata. Ci sono per questo meno strumenti per contrastarne la diffusione: non esistono per esempio vaccini né trattamenti specifici, anche se sono in corso delle sperimentazioni . Per ora l’unico modo di contenerla è quello di individuare tempestivamente i malati, isolarli e curarli.

items.title: Trump and Zelensky at loggerheads despite new optimism
items.summary: The Ukrainian leader's hug with Steve Witkoff in the Norwegian capital is unlikely to dispel misgivings about US policy towards his country, writes Paul Adams.
items.content:
The hug that Trump envoy Steve Witkoff offered Volodymyr Zelensky before talks in Oslo is unlikely to have dispelled the Ukrainian leader's misgivings about the current direction of US policy towards his war-ravaged country.

Zelensky posted a video of the moment on social media, with the message "Ukraine is working for peace. I thank our partners for their support!"

But given everything that's happened this month, does the Ukrainian leader still regard Donald Trump as a partner?

The two men have never been close – that much is obvious – but have they now fallen out once and for all?

Both in rhetoric and actions, the past 10 days have seen evidence of a rupture as deep as any in their fractious relationship.

"Zelensky's not a good guy for us to deal with," Trump told Newsmax last week.

"Zelensky doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump told a reporter on Monday when asked what he thought of the Ukrainian leader's suggestion that striking a diesel deal with Russia put the US on the wrong side of history.

Such personal attacks are typical of Trump's sledgehammer approach to diplomacy. It's hard to know when to take them seriously.

In June, he lashed out at Israel's prime minister, using an expletive while criticising Benjamin Netanyahu's judgement. Four months later, he endorsed Netanyahu enthusiastically, calling him a "great warrior prime minister".

"Trump can always do another U-turn," says Ian Bond of the Centre for European Reform. "But this does look bad."

For his part Zelensky has generally been circumspect in how he describes his unreliable but vital American counterpart.

But this month his frustration has been clear. Addressing a US congressional delegation, he spoke of "decisions on the American side that are hard to explain between friends" and voiced the fear that "some political decision has been made to slow down support for us."

Answering Trump's charge that he represented the principal obstacle to a negotiated settlement, Zelensky sounded more exasperated than ever.

"We have welcomed literally EVERY attempt by our partners to end this war with dignity," he wrote on Telegram on Monday.

After their notorious televised bust up in the Oval Office in February 2025, at which Trump accused Zelensky of "gambling with World War III", the US suspended military assistance and restricted intelligence sharing.

The crisis only lasted a week. And when the Trump administration decided, later that year, that it no longer wanted to finance direct military assistance to Ukraine, a mechanism was put in place for European countries to pay for American equipment instead.

One exception, in the wake of this year's US war with Iran, has been badly needed US-made Patriot air defence missiles.

Amid a global shortage, the supply to Ukraine has slowed to a trickle, making it harder than ever for Kyiv to shoot down Russian ballistic missiles.

The Washington Post, quoting an unnamed Ukrainian official, said "only a couple" of Patriot interceptors remained in Ukraine's stockpile, and that the Trump administration had slowed down the process by which US allies seek approval to transfer their stocks.

Similar concerns have been voiced in the past, but the latest reports – not confirmed by US officials – come against an increasingly difficult backdrop for Kyiv.

Earlier this month, as Ukrainian negotiators arrived in Miami for talks with Trump's all-purpose envoys Witkoff and Jared Kushner, they were blindsided by the news that the president had just struck a deal with Vladimir Putin to open US markets to Russian diesel.

Experts questioned whether it would do much to drive down US petrol prices, ahead of congressional mid-term elections (the apparent motive), but as a signal of US displeasure over Ukraine's campaign of long-range strikes on Russian oil refineries and Washington's willingness to do deals with the Kremlin, it represented a stinging rebuke to Kyiv.

Last Friday, Trump went further, waiving wide-ranging sanctions on Russia just two days before they were due to take effect.

Trump said the sanctions contained in the Graham Act (named after the former South Carolina senator Lindsey Graham, a vocal supporter of Ukraine who died in July) would hinder his efforts to broker peace. But for Kyiv and its supporters this was another alarming sign that the White House was siding with the Kremlin.

"What the Trump administration is doing is providing carrots to the Russians and sticks to the Ukrainians," former US ambassador to Kyiv William Taylor told the BBC.

Kiriil Dmitriev, a senior Putin envoy, called it "an important and truly historic moment".

For Moscow, this felt like a welcome return to the "spirit of Alaska", a phrase much touted by Russian officials in the wake of the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage in August 2025.

Adding to the impression that Trump is turning his back on Ukraine is the allegation – again not confirmed by Washington – that the US has restricted the flow of intelligence and interfered with Ukraine's access to Elon Musk's Starlink satellite internet service.

Amid an escalation in Russia's drone and missile war on Ukraine's cities, Kyiv says advance warning provided by US satellite intelligence has been lacking.

"We didn't receive it during ballistic attacks for three days," Zelensky told NBC News.

On 12 October five Russian S-400 missiles hit Kyiv, reportedly before air raid sirens or mobile alerts had sounded.

The US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, denied there had been any pause in intelligence sharing, blaming a "software problem" for the temporary lack of early warnings.

Similar uncertainty surrounds Ukraine's access to Starlink .

A week ago, Ukrainian officials reported that the system was being throttled, with terminals unable to maintain connections at high speeds, making it harder for Ukraine's military to intercept fast moving Russian drones.

Since the summer, Ukraine has struggled to cope with a wave of attacks by advanced, jet-powered drones.

It's not clear where any order to limit Ukraine's use of Starlink – or its military grade equivalent Starshield – originated. Reuters reported that it came from the White House.

Rubio said "no-one at the White House ordered anyone to slow down internet."

But the fact that such suspicions surface so frequently points to the lack of trust that continues to infect US-Ukrainian relations.

Much of this has its roots in Donald Trump's seemingly long-standing mistrust of Ukraine as a whole - and Zelensky in particular.

A decade ago, Trump became convinced that Ukraine had tried to prevent him from becoming US president. Among a number of unfounded allegations was the suggestion that the US Democratic National Committee had a server hidden somewhere in Ukraine.

When Zelensky became president, three years later, he resisted Trump's demands that he investigate charges of election interference.

During a notorious July 2019 telephone conversation, Trump also asked Zelensky to investigate Joe Biden, the man who went on to defeat him in the 2020 presidential election. Again, Zelensky refused.

At the time, the White House was withholding $391m (£290m) in military assistance to Ukraine, a juxtaposition that ultimately led to Trump's first impeachment.

Whether Trump's resentment over these historic slights continues to inform his current policy towards Ukraine is an open question, but it's clear that the roller coaster of US-Ukraine relations has taken another stomach-churning dip.

Following the talks in Oslo, Witkoff is taking a set of updated proposals to St Petersburg. All eyes will now be on Putin.

Jonas Gahr Støre, the Norwegian leader, said the talks in Oslo had helped "to straighten out a few things."

"There's nothing to gain from… digging into what was said yesterday or a week ago," he said diplomatically.

Zelensky said the day had begun with a productive conversation with the US Secretary of State and indicated that the issue of early warning had already been fixed. He also sounded optimistic about Patriot missiles and Starlink.

Yet despite the optimistic tone, it's hard to get around the fact that Volodymyr Zelensky and Donald Trump appear, once again, to be at loggerheads.

items.title: Trump sued over Canadian tariffs in latest legal challenge
items.summary: The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the latest tariffs on the country and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".
items.content:
US President Donald Trump is facing another legal challenge on tariffs after the group that successfully sued over his so-called "liberation day" import taxes filed a new lawsuit over the latest Canadian levies.

The White House imposed a 50% levy on some $20bn of Canadian goods after trade talks between the US and Canada broke down in August.

The Liberty Justice Center filed a suit on behalf of US food business Gellert Global Group, urging the US Court of International Trade to find the levies unlawful and to order refunds with interest for affected importers.

The lawsuit argues the White House exceeded its authority in imposing the tariffs and caused "immediate harm to American businesses".

Gellert Global Group is a third-generation family business that is paying 50% tariffs on cheese exported from Canada. The New Jersey-based firm is also facing retaliatory tariffs from Canada on American-made cheese it sells north of the border.

Co-chief executive Thomas Gellert said the firm had spent generations building relationships with suppliers and customers in the food industry.

"These tariffs disrupt those relationships overnight and create costs and uncertainty that ripple through the entire supply chain," he said on Tuesday.

The Liberty Justice Center is challenging the administration's use of Section 338 of the 1930 Tariff Act to hit Canadian goods from wine to dairy products and hockey sticks.

That section of the nearly 100-year-old Act is aimed at protecting US business against foreign discrimination, but the legal group is arguing that it does not allow the executive branch "to impose sweeping tariffs or import restrictions whenever a trade dispute arises".

The lawsuit seeks to challenge the White House's reliance on retaliatory tariffs imposed by Canada to justify its own duties under Section 338.

Canada has imposed a series of countermeasures against numerous US tariffs. Last month, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney matched the Section 338 US tariffs "dollar for dollar" after Trump imposed them for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol.

It also points out Section 338 requires a 30-day waiting period before levies can be imposed, but the tariff on products including cheese was added to the list just a week before tariff collection began.

Sara Albrecht, chief executive of the Liberty Justice Center, said the case was not about Trump himself but about the presidency.

"No president should have the power to pull a dormant statute off the shelf and use it to impose sweeping tariffs or import bans without the limits Congress required," she said.

The lawsuit argues that Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 has been superseded by Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.

It also argues that if Section 338 still applies, the White House has not established the legal basis for the sweeping tariffs against Canada.

"The case is not an objection to tariffs as such. It asks who has the power to impose them and whether the executive branch followed the law Congress wrote," the Liberty Justice Center said.

The law group has also filed a motion for a preliminary injunction to block their collection.

It is the fourth case brought by the group against Trump's tariffs, including its successful case against the sweeping tariffs brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) that were struck down in February this year.

Albrecht said the group had brought all the cases for the same reason: "the Constitution gives tariff power to Congress. The executive branch cannot keep moving the same policy from one statute to another and pretend the limits disappear".

'Half my business will be gone' - firms in Canada and US fear trade war

items.title: Dal 20 ottobre si può fare domanda per il bonus per le madri che lavorano
items.content: Da martedì 20 ottobre è possibile fare domanda per ricevere il cosiddetto “ bonus mamme ”, cioè il contributo per le madri che hanno lavorato nel 2026. Il contributo è di 60 euro al mese (rispetto ai 40 del 2025) e arriva al massimo a 720 euro, erogati in un’unica soluzione. Può essere chiesto dalle madri che hanno due figli, di cui il più piccolo fino a nove anni, o madri con almeno tre figli, di cui il più piccolo minorenne. Le madri devono avere anche un reddito annuo inferiore a 40mila euro, con contratti di lavoro dipendente (sia nel pubblico che nel privato) o essere lavoratrici autonome. Sono escluse le collaboratrici domestiche.

items.title: Da Ghali a Fedez, i rapper si schierano sugli scontri in piazza
items.summary: Marracash: "Mai inneggiato alla violenza. Avere i soldi non mi impedisce di lottare"
items.content:
La condanna della violenza, ma anche la voglia di dare voce al disagio sociale, al desiderio di riscatto di chi cresce tra insuccessi e sogno di ricchezza: il mondo del rap italiano, che ormai domina le classifiche e colleziona record di streaming (e di fatturato), si interroga sugli scontri che hanno scosso Milano e altre città d'Italia . E prende posizione con voci diverse, tra sostegno a una generazione a caccia di futuro, disapprovazione per il vandalismo gratuito e autocritica.

Ad aprire il dibattito è stato Marracash: "Con le buone non cambi le cose", ha scritto ieri sui social il rapper della Barona. Vicino alle sue posizioni è Sayf: "Ci dicono che il problema sono le manifestazioni violente, ma chi sta togliendo alle persone il diritto a un futuro dignitoso?", riflette l'artista, secondo a Sanremo 2026 con Tu mi piaci tanto. "Si dimentica la violenza di un sistema che mette il profitto sopra la vita e la dignità delle persone, perché il problema n on è la divisione tra destra e sinistra, ma quella tra chi sta sopra e chi sta sotto e noi siamo tutti dalla stessa parte: quella di chi sta sotto ". Quelle sulle diseguaglianze sociali "sono risposte che i giovani stanno cercando di ottenere ormai da un po'. Secondo me dobbiamo ascoltarli", sottolinea Ghali, che si dice "contento che le persone stiano scendendo in piazza a manifestare il proprio diritto e a cercare delle risposte" e invita a usare "questo tempo per parlare di chi sta manifestando pacificamente, perché è la vera cosa. Non distraiamoci". Per Nayt, "siccome in questo mondo viviamo insieme, a un certo punto, se non vedi l'altro, l'altro ti entrerà in casa per essere visto. Tutto questo finto benessere materiale ha reso borghesi anche i più poveri. Poverini e poveracci".

Opposta la valutazione di Fedez: "Conosco la frustrazione di una casa brutta in periferia, di un lavoro o di una scuola del ca**o, di non poterti comprare niente di bello. Conosco pure l'adrenalina di quando invece i soldi arrivano, la soddisfazione di poter far vedere agli altri dove sei arrivato. Per questo le vetrine del centro di Milano sono il bersaglio perfetto: rappresentano il simbolo tangibile di tutto ciò che a quei ragazzi è precluso. Vedo anche artisti e personaggi pubblici che celebrano la protesta , ci si uniscono come se ne facessero parte, senza rendersi conto che esposti in quelle vetrine ci sono anche loro. A promuovere quella idea di vita e di successo ci siamo noi. Siamo noi che andiamo alle sfilate, postiamo gli orologi di lusso, i viaggi e i vestiti". Un'allusione, probabilmente, a Ghali, tra i protagonisti delle ultime passerelle milanesi. Luchè sceglie il suo brano Se non ci fosse la rabbia e scrive "Non voglio unione / Voglio divisione / Combatto con chi ha / La mia stessa missione", mentre Nerone invita a distinguere tra "milioni di persone" che "stanno protestando pacificamente per cercare di farsi sentire da sti merda mangiasoldi" e "400 clown minorenni con le squalo e i buchi nel cervello" che "hanno sfondato negozi e auto come le peggiori delle bestie".

Se Guè e Artie 5ive siglano con il loro like il post di Marracash, quest'ultimo risponde alle critiche di chi ha letto nelle sue parole un incitamento alla violenza : "Ok, mi sono preso una vagonata di merda, ci sta, me lo aspettavo", scrive oggi in un lungo post. Ma "un paio di cose non mi stanno bene" , spiega. "La prima è che non ho mai inneggiato alla violenza", "ma quando questa violenza succede, bisogna farsi delle domande", perché pur nella follia del gesto è sintomo "di un fallimento della società di cui tutti siamo responsabili" . "Un risentimento crescente sta maturando in tutti", "per ora riguarda le classi più deboli e ai margini, le periferie e le seconde generazioni, ma sta crescendo anche nel ceto medio che manifesta pacificamente". Marracash respinge anche "la retorica del 'tu hai i soldi, non puoi parlare'". "Aver fatto i soldi non cancella più di metà della mia vita e soprattutto non mi impedisce di lottare per un mondo più equo e più giusto per tutti, né di lottare per questo".
